title: Anatomy of a great prompt
subtitle: Four ingredients. Drop one, and the AI invents it for you.
cliffhanger: Tomorrow: give the AI a role. The quality of everything shifts.

paragraphs: You're back. And you're somewhere new.
Path 1 was about teaching you to **think**. How I execute, what [[term:contesto]]context[[/term]] is, why [[term:vincoli]]constraints[[/term]] save you. Now we change craft.
From here on we work on the message. The thing you actually type into the box. It's called a [[term:prompt]]prompt[[/term]], and it can be written well or badly — that's not an opinion.

vignettes.full: You finished a whole Path. Few people get this far. I'm not saying it to flatter you, I'm saying it because it's a fact.
In Path 1 we thought. From now on we write. It's more hands-on and, I'll say it, more fun.

paragraphs: Most people treat a prompt like a Google search. Three words, enter, fingers crossed.
But I'm not a search engine. I don't give you back **the right page**: I build you **what you described**. If the description is thin, what you get is thin too.
A well-made prompt looks like something else. Two steps from now I'll tell you what.

vignettes.full: On Google you search. With me you describe. It's a small distinction to say and a huge one to do.
Three words are enough to search. To build, no. Almost never.

paragraphs: Let me show you what I mean. Lucia — the one with the site from Path 1 — writes me one day: «make me a contact page».
And I made her one. A title saying «Contact», three fields, a grey button. Technically correct. Useless.
I didn't know it was for her photography studio. I didn't know she wanted the requests sent to an email via Resend. I didn't know it had to match her style. I didn't ask: I invented it. Badly.
Result: Lucia rewrote the prompt three times. Forty minutes for a contact page. The problem wasn't me. It was the first message.

vignettes.full: Everything you don't tell me, I make up. And when I make things up, I get your taste wrong almost every time.
Forty minutes for a contact page. It could have been written in one prompt, done right.

steps.headline: A prompt isn't a question.
steps.caption: A brief is what you'd hand a sharp collaborator who just walked in: they know nothing about the project until you tell them. Treat me the same way.

vignettes.full: I'm sharp, yes. But about you and your project, I know nothing. Every time I start from scratch.
You write the brief. I execute it. If the brief is clear, the rest follows on its own.

paragraphs: A well-made brief has four ingredients. Always the same four.

**Context** — what you're building and where this piece fits in. **Task** — what I have to do, precisely. **Constraints** — the [[term:stack]]stack[[/term]], the libraries, and what I must NOT touch. **Format** — how you want the answer back: ready-to-paste code? a plan first? an explanation?
Four. Not seven, not two. And now I'll tell you something you'll like.

vignettes.full: Context, task, constraints, format. The project changes — the ingredients don't.
You don't have to use all four every time. But every time you should **know** which ones you're leaving out.

paragraphs: Two of these four you already know. We did them together in Path 1.

**Context** is Lesson 3 — the four layers: project, code, constraints, examples. **Constraints** is Lesson 4 — protective, process, style. I won't re-explain them. When they show up, you'll recognise them.
So in this lesson we focus on the two new ones: the **precise task** and the **output format**. They're the ones almost everyone forgets.

vignettes.full: Two ingredients out of four you've already learned. You hadn't noticed, had you?
Task and format. They're the two people always skip. Starting today, not you.

steps.prompt: Three people ask the AI the same thing. Which prompt do you expect to work best?

options.label: «Make me a reviews section for my site, done well.»

«Add a customer reviews section to my B&B landing page (Next.js, /components/sections already exists). Three static reviews with name, stars, text. Don't add libraries. Give me just the component, with one comment per block.»
«Add a reviews section following best practices and making it professional and modern.»

vignettes.full: Read all three in full before you pick. One is polite, one is full of buzzwords, one is right.

paragraphs: The right prompt was the second one.

It had all four ingredients: context (B&B, Next.js, /components/sections), precise task (three static reviews with name, stars, text), constraints (no libraries), format (just the component, one comment per block).

complete: The right prompt was the second one. And you picked it.

It had all four ingredients: context (B&B, Next.js, /components/sections), precise task (three static reviews with name, stars, text), constraints (no libraries), format (just the component, one comment per block).
Means you've already got the eye for the four ingredients. Now I'll take them apart one by one.
polite: The right prompt was the second one, not the first.
The first was **polite**. «Done well» isn't an instruction, it's a wish. I don't know what «done well» means for you: I make it up.
The second had all four ingredients — context, precise task, constraints, format. Let me take them apart one by one now.
buzzwords: The right prompt was the second one, not the third.
The third sounded the most «professional», didn't it? That's the trap. «Best practices», «modern», «professional» don't mean anything concrete — I fill them in however I like.
The second had all four ingredients — context, precise task, constraints, format. Let me take them apart one by one now.

vignettes.full: «Do well», «do it carefully», «make it professional»: those are wishes. Nice. Useless to me.
The vaguer a word is, the more I fill it in from my own head. And my head isn't yours.

paragraphs: First new ingredient: the **task**. It seems the most obvious. It's the one written worst, most often.
«Add authentication» is not a task. It's a category. Inside it are a hundred decisions that — if you don't make them — I make.
«Implement Google login using Supabase Auth, and after login send the user to /dashboard» — **this** is a task. It has a verb, an object, an observable outcome.
The test: after reading the task, is there still something I'd have to decide? If yes, it's not a task yet. It's a title.

vignettes.full: A real task has a verb, an object, and an outcome you can see. If one is missing, it's vague.
«Add authentication» is a category. «Google login, redirect to /dashboard» is a task. Feel the difference?

paragraphs: Second new ingredient, and the most forgotten of them all: the **output format**. That is, **how** you want the answer back.

The exact same request can come back in wildly different shapes. Do you want ready-to-paste code? Do you want me to give you a plan first and wait for your go-ahead? Do you want a line-by-line explanation because you're learning? Three different answers to the same question.
If you don't say, I choose. And maybe I comment everything when you just wanted the code, or I dump three hundred lines on you when you wanted a plan first.
One line. «Give me a plan first, then wait.» It changes the whole session.

vignettes.full: The same thing I can give you as code, as a plan, or as an explanation. You decide, or I decide.
Format is the ingredient nobody writes. Writing it sets you apart right away.

steps.headline: Every ingredient you drop,
steps.emphasis: the AI decides in your place.
steps.caption: And the decisions I make are exactly the ones you end up rewriting. There's a fifth element that amplifies all of this — giving me a role — but that's tomorrow's lesson.

vignettes.full: There's one thing that powers all four ingredients at once. It's called a «role». Tomorrow.
Look at the times you've had to redo an output: almost always it was a decision I made because you didn't write it down.

paragraphs: One clarification, before we wrap. I'm not telling you to write a poem every time.

Short prompts work great when context is **already established**: inside an ongoing session, or when you have a [[term:claude-md]]CLAUDE.md[[/term]] keeping me up to date (you remember from Lesson 2). There, «move it to the right» is plenty.
Full anatomy is for when I open something new and non-trivial. The practical test stays the same: is there anything I'd have to invent? If yes, write it.

vignettes.full: In an ongoing session a short prompt is fine — I already have the context. The problem is cold starts.
If you've got a good CLAUDE.md, part of the context is already written. The prompt can be shorter. You did the work earlier.

steps.intro: Now it's on you. I'll give you a scenario and a vague prompt — the kind anyone would write. You rewrite it well, ingredient by ingredient. What you write you keep: it's the first piece of your prompt library.

scenario.brief: A padel court booking app. It already exists, built on Next.js with Supabase. The page the manager sees when they log in is missing.
scenario.vague_prompt: make me a dashboard for the manager
scenario.generic_output: A generic dashboard: three boxes «Stat 1», «Stat 2», «Stat 3», a fake chart with random values, zero connection to padel.
scenario.spark_intro_line: Technically it's a dashboard. But it isn't YOURS. Let's rewrite the prompt that produced it — one ingredient at a time.

context.question: What are you building, and where does this piece fit?

tiles.label: A dashboard for my app
tiles.coaching: Readable but vague — I'd fill the gaps in however I like.

tiles.label: The manager dashboard of a padel court booking app on Next.js + Supabase
tiles.coaching: Specific. Now I know exactly where you're plugging in.

tiles.label: A modern and professional dashboard
tiles.coaching: Sounds good and says nothing. That's the trap.

task.question: What should the dashboard do? Be precise: verb, object, outcome.
task.placeholder: E.g. show today's booking count and a chart of bookings per day for the last week…

constraints.question: What must the AI NOT touch? Pick two.

tiles.label: Don't add libraries beyond Recharts
tiles.coaching: Specific, protective. Cuts off any temptation to import half of npm.

tiles.label: Show me a plan before writing code
tiles.coaching: Real process constraint. Forces me to stop and show you.

tiles.label: Reuse the components already in /components
tiles.coaching: Concrete project anchor. No new code duplicating what exists.

tiles.label: Do clean, professional work
tiles.coaching: A wish, not a constraint. «Clean» I interpret myself, and badly.

format.question: How do you want the answer back?

tiles.label: A plan first, then wait for my go-ahead
tiles.coaching: You give me a check-in gate. Good.

tiles.label: Code, please
tiles.coaching: Ok but how much code? With or without comments? I decide.

tiles.label: However you prefer
tiles.coaching: «However you prefer» means however I prefer. You decide.

anatomy_config.model_answer:
CONTEXT: The manager dashboard of a padel court booking app on Next.js + Supabase. It's the home after the manager's login.
TASK: Show today's booking count and a chart of bookings per day for the last week, so the manager can see at a glance whether the week is holding.
CONSTRAINTS: Don't add libraries beyond Recharts · Show me a plan before writing code
FORMAT: A plan first, then wait for my go-ahead.

vignettes.full: One box per ingredient. Fill them all. If you leave one blank, I'll tell you.
Three tries. On the second I'll tell you what's weak; on the third I'll spell it out.
The prompt you assemble you take home. Reuse it on your next real project, changing the details.

paragraphs: First lesson of Path 2, done. Now you know what a prompt is made of inside — and you've got one of your own, written by you.

Tomorrow we add one thing, and it sounds like a small trick: I'll have you give me a **role**. «Act as a security expert», «you're a copywriter». The quality of what I give back shifts on the spot — and I'll explain why it isn't magic.
See you there.

vignettes.full: That prompt you just wrote is piece number one. You build from here.
The role sounds like a small thing. It's among the most powerful I'll teach you. See you tomorrow.
